goals: Draw and label a typical flower and describe it by symmetry, merous condition and completeness
Identify the types of aestivation of the calyx and corolla

slides.heading: The flower and its parts
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the four whorls of a flower, and how the outer whorls and the stamens are described.

visual.alt: Four whorls arranged on the thalamus from outside to inside: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium

slides.narration: The flower is the reproductive shoot of a flowering plant. Its parts are arranged in rings, called whorls, on the swollen tip of the stalk, the thalamus. From outside to inside they are the calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.

slides.heading: A typical flower
slides.body_md: A flower sits on a stalk, the **pedicel**. The **calyx** (sepals) and **corolla** (petals) are the non-essential whorls; the **androecium** (stamens) and **gynoecium** (carpels) are the essential whorls.

visual.alt: A flower in longitudinal section with pedicel, thalamus, sepals, petals, stamens and carpel

slides.narration: The outer green sepals form the calyx, and the coloured petals form the corolla. Inside are the stamens, each with a filament and an anther that holds pollen. At the centre is the carpel, with a stigma to receive pollen, a style, and an ovary containing ovules.

slides.heading: Bracteate, ebracteate and symmetry
slides.body_md: Flowers are described by whether a **bract** is present and by how they can be cut into equal halves.

rows: A small leaf, the bract, arises at the base of the pedicel
No bract at the base of the pedicel
Radially symmetrical: cut into equal halves by any vertical plane through the centre
Bilaterally symmetrical: equal halves by one vertical plane only
No vertical plane gives equal halves

visual.alt: Table of bracteate, ebracteate, actinomorphic, zygomorphic and asymmetric flowers with examples

slides.narration: A flower with a bract at the base of its stalk is bracteate; one without is ebracteate. A radially symmetrical flower such as datura can be halved in many planes. A zygomorphic flower such as gulmohar has just one plane, and an asymmetric flower such as canna has none.

slides.heading: Merous condition; complete and incomplete flowers
slides.body_md: The number of members in each whorl gives the **merous** condition. A flower with all four whorls is **complete**; one that lacks any whorl is **incomplete**.

rows: Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium all present
Male flower of pumpkin: no gynoecium

visual.alt: Table of merous condition and of complete and incomplete flowers

slides.narration: Count the members in each whorl. Threes make the flower trimerous, fours tetramerous, fives pentamerous. A flower is complete only when all four whorls are present. The male flower of the pumpkin has no carpels, so it is incomplete.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: describing a flower
slides.body_md: A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 5 stamens and 2 carpels. It can be cut into equal halves by many planes. Describe it.
bullets: Five sepals, five petals and five stamens: the whorls are in fives, so it is **pentamerous**.
Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium are all present: it is a **complete** flower.
Equal halves along many vertical planes: **actinomorphic**.
Members altogether: 5 + 5 + 5 + 2 = 17; of these 7 belong to the essential whorls.

visual.alt: Worked table: 17 members in all

slides.narration: Take the description in steps. First count the members in each whorl, then see whether every whorl is there, then test the symmetry. This flower is pentamerous, complete and radially symmetrical, with seventeen members in all, seven of them in the essential whorls.

slides.heading: Calyx, corolla and perianth
slides.body_md: The sepals may be free (**polysepalous**) or joined (**gamosepalous**); the petals free (**polypetalous**) or joined (**gamopetalous**). When the calyx and corolla look alike they form a **perianth**, whose members are tepals.

visual.alt: Table of free and joined sepals and petals

slides.narration: Joined members carry the prefix gamo, free ones the prefix poly. In a lily the calyx and corolla cannot be told apart, and together they are called the perianth, whose six parts are tepals.

slides.heading: Aestivation
slides.body_md: **Aestivation** is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud, in relation to one another.

slides.narration: Most anthers are bilobed, or dithecous, with two lobes joined by the connective and four pollen sacs in all. The kidney-shaped anther of hibiscus and cotton has a single lobe, so it is monothecous, with just two pollen sacs.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting pollen sacs
slides.body_md: A hibiscus flower has 60 stamens, each monothecous. A sunflower floret has 5 stamens, each dithecous. Find the pollen sacs in each.
bullets: A monothecous anther has 2 pollen sacs, so the hibiscus flower has 60 × 2 = 120.
A dithecous anther has 4 pollen sacs, so the floret has 5 × 4 = 20.
If the hibiscus anthers were dithecous the flower would have 240, twice as many.

visual.alt: Worked table: 120 pollen sacs in hibiscus, 20 in a sunflower floret

slides.narration: Multiply the number of stamens by the number of pollen sacs in one anther. A monothecous anther has two, a dithecous one has four. So sixty monothecous stamens give one hundred twenty sacs, and five dithecous stamens give twenty.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium on the thalamus.
Described by bract, symmetry (actinomorphic, zygomorphic, asymmetric), merous condition and completeness.
Calyx and corolla: gamo- or poly-; perianth when alike; aestivation valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary.
Stamens: cohesion (mono-, di-, polyadelphous, syngenesious), adhesion (epipetalous, epiphyllous).
Anthers: dithecous (four sacs) or monothecous (two sacs).

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say **which** whorl is missing when you call a flower incomplete.
Give an **example** with every term: pea for diadelphous, sunflower for syngenesious, hibiscus for monadelphous.
Do not mix **cohesion** (stamens with stamens) and **adhesion** (stamens with another whorl).
Count pollen sacs: **four** in a dithecous anther, **two** in a monothecous one.

visual.alt: The carpel from stigma through style to the ovary that holds the ovules

slides.narration: A carpel has three parts: the stigma, which receives pollen, the style, and the swollen ovary at the base. The ovary holds the ovules, which become seeds. Flowers themselves are arranged on the shoot in a pattern called the inflorescence.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: order of opening
slides.body_md: A radish raceme has 24 flowers; one opens every 2 days, starting from the base. (a) How many days separate the opening of the lowest and the topmost flower? (b) How many flowers are open on day 20? A jasmine cyme has 9 flowers; the first opens on day 0 and one more every 3 days. (c) On which day does the youngest open?
bullets: (a) 23 gaps × 2 days = **46 days**.
(b) Flowers opened by day 20: 20 ÷ 2 + 1 = **11**, leaving 13 buds.
(c) 8 gaps × 3 days = day **24**.

slides.narration: With a number of flowers, there is one gap less than the number of flowers. Multiply the gaps by the interval to find the time between the first and the last. To count open flowers, divide the day by the interval and add the flower that opened on day zero.

Placentation: axile, parietal, free central, basal, marginal.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In a diagram of a flower, look at **where the other whorls arise** to name the ovary position.
For placentation, count the **chambers** first, then see where the ovules are attached.
Compare racemose and cymose on **two points**: main axis and order of opening.
Do **not** write the subtypes of inflorescence; they are not in the syllabus.

sections.heading: 1. The flower: structure, symmetry, merous condition
sections.body_md:
The **flower** is the reproductive unit of an angiosperm: a modified shoot of limited growth. It sits on a stalk, the **pedicel**, whose swollen tip, the **thalamus** (receptacle), bears four **whorls**: **calyx** (sepals), **corolla** (petals), **androecium** (stamens) and **gynoecium** (carpels). The calyx and corolla are the **non-essential** (accessory) whorls; the androecium and gynoecium are the **essential** whorls, because they produce the gametes. A flower is drawn in longitudinal section with the parts labelled: pedicel, thalamus, sepal, petal, stamen (filament and anther), carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules).

**Bract.** A small leaf at the base of the pedicel is a **bract**. A flower with a bract is **bracteate** (Bougainvillea); one without is **ebracteate** (mustard).

**Symmetry.** An **actinomorphic** (regular) flower can be cut into two equal halves by any vertical plane through the centre (datura, lily). A **zygomorphic** (bilaterally symmetrical) flower can be so cut in **one** plane only (gulmohar, bean, pea). An **asymmetric** (irregular) flower cannot be cut into equal halves by any vertical plane (canna).

**Merous condition.** If the members of each whorl are in threes the flower is **trimerous** (typical of monocots, for example lily: 6 tepals, 6 stamens and 3 carpels, 15 members in all); in fours, **tetramerous** (mustard); in fives, **pentamerous** (typical of dicots).

**Complete and incomplete.** A flower with all four whorls is **complete**; if one or more whorls are missing it is **incomplete**. A flower with both stamens and carpels is **bisexual**; one with only one of them is **unisexual** (the male flower of pumpkin has no gynoecium, so it is incomplete).

sections.heading: 2. Calyx, corolla and aestivation
sections.body_md:
The **calyx** is made of **sepals**, usually green, which protect the bud. If the sepals are free the calyx is **polysepalous**; if joined, **gamosepalous**. The **corolla** is made of **petals**, usually coloured, which attract pollinators; free petals make it **polypetalous**, joined petals **gamopetalous**. When the calyx and corolla cannot be told apart, as in lily, the two whorls together form a **perianth**, and its members are **tepals**.

**Aestivation** is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud, in relation to the other members of the same whorl.
- **Valvate** — the margins of adjacent members just touch without overlapping (*Calotropis*).
- **Twisted** — one margin of each member overlaps the next, and the other is overlapped by the previous one (cotton, okra).
- **Imbricate** — the margins overlap in no definite direction; one member is wholly outside and one wholly inside (gulmohar, *Cassia*).
- **Vexillary** (papilionaceous) — the large posterior petal, the **standard**, overlaps the two lateral **wings**, which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals, the **keel** (pea, bean).

Books differ in how finely they describe imbricate and twisted aestivation; the four types above are those named in the syllabus.

Arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud.
Aestivation with a standard, two wings and a keel, as in pea.
Members meet edge to edge without overlapping.

sections.heading: 3. Androecium: cohesion, adhesion and anthers
sections.body_md:
The **androecium** is made of **stamens**; each has a **filament** and an **anther**, in which pollen grains are formed. Stamens may be free or united.

**Cohesion** (union of stamens with each other):
- **Monadelphous** — filaments joined in one bundle (hibiscus, cotton).
- **Diadelphous** — filaments in two bundles; in the pea and bean, 9 are joined and 1 is free.
- **Polyadelphous** — filaments in more than two bundles (*Bombax*, citrus, castor).
- **Syngenesious** — anthers joined, filaments free (sunflower).
- **Synandrous** — filaments and anthers all joined (pumpkin, cucumber).

**Adhesion** (union of stamens with another whorl): **epipetalous** — stamens attached to the petals (datura, brinjal, sunflower florets); **epiphyllous** — attached to the tepals (lily).

**Anthers.** A **dithecous** anther has two lobes (**thecae**) joined by a **connective**, each with two **pollen sacs**, so four pollen sacs in all (sunflower, most flowers). A **monothecous** anther is kidney shaped, with one lobe and two pollen sacs (hibiscus, cotton). A hibiscus flower with sixty stamens therefore has 120 pollen sacs.

*Where books differ.* Some books describe the pollen sacs of a monothecous anther as fused into a single chamber; the notes follow the two-sac description used with the syllabus.

sections.heading: 4. Gynoecium: ovary position, carpels and placentation
sections.body_md:
The **gynoecium** is made of one or more **carpels** (pistils); each has a **stigma**, a **style** and an **ovary** with **ovules**. If the carpels are **free** the gynoecium is **apocarpous** (lotus, rose); if **fused**, **syncarpous** (tomato, cotton). The ovary of a syncarpous gynoecium is divided into chambers called **locules**.

**Position of the ovary.**
- **Hypogynous** — the ovary is **superior**; the other whorls arise below it (mustard, datura, tomato).
- **Perigynous** — the ovary is **half-inferior**, in a cup-shaped thalamus whose rim bears the other whorls (rose, plum).
- **Epigynous** — the ovary is **inferior**; the thalamus fuses with it and the other whorls arise above it (sunflower, cucumber).

**Placentation** is the arrangement of ovules on the **placenta**.
- **Axile** — ovules on the central axis of a chambered ovary (tomato, lemon, lily).
- **Parietal** — ovules on the inner wall of a one-chambered ovary (mustard, *Argemone*, cucumber).
- **Free central** — ovules on a central column without partitions (*Dianthus*, primrose).
- **Basal** — a single ovule at the base of a one-chambered ovary (sunflower, marigold).
- **Marginal** — ovules along one margin of a one-carpelled ovary (pea, bean).

*Where books differ.* A few plants are placed differently in different books (for example the position of the pea ovary), so the notes use the examples listed above.

sections.heading: 5. Inflorescence: racemose and cymose
sections.body_md:
The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is the **inflorescence**. Its two main kinds differ in the main axis and in the order of opening of flowers.
- **Racemose** — the main axis **keeps growing** and bears flowers laterally in an **acropetal** order: the **oldest flowers are at the base** and the **youngest near the tip** (radish, golden shower tree).
- **Cymose** — the main axis **ends in a flower**, so its growth is limited; the flowers are borne in a **basipetal** order: the **oldest flower is at the top** and the **younger ones below** (jasmine, Bougainvillea).

*Removed from the syllabus:* the subtypes of racemose and cymose inflorescence are not required. A raceme of 24 flowers in which one flower opens every two days has the topmost flower opening 46 days after the lowest.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling a flower with no gynoecium "complete"; it is incomplete (and unisexual).
- Mixing **cohesion** (stamens with stamens) and **adhesion** (stamens with petals or tepals).
- Writing the pea as monadelphous; it is diadelphous (nine joined, one free).
- Saying a dithecous anther has two pollen sacs; it has four.
- Naming the ovary position from the number of carpels instead of from where the other whorls arise.
- Giving parietal placentation for a chambered ovary with ovules on the axis; that is axile.
- Writing that in a raceme the youngest flower is at the base.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term for a condition, an example plant, a lettered figure, a give-a-reason.
- 2- and 3-mark questions: actinomorphic against zygomorphic; cohesion against adhesion; racemose against cymose; two types of placentation with examples.
- 5-mark questions in parts: a labelled diagram of a flower in L.S.; aestivation with examples; ovary position and placentation.

questions.solution_md: One plane only means zygomorphic; many planes mean actinomorphic — option (c).

questions.solution_md: A flower with a bract at the base of the pedicel is bracteate — option (a).

questions.solution_md: False: such a flower, for example canna, is asymmetric; a zygomorphic flower can be divided by one plane.

questions.solution_md: Essential.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A zygomorphic flower can be cut into two equal halves by only one vertical plane.

**Reason (R):** A zygomorphic flower is radially symmetrical.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: a zygomorphic flower is bilaterally symmetrical; radial symmetry belongs to an actinomorphic flower — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A pumpkin flower that has no stamens is an incomplete flower.

**Reason (R):** A complete flower has the calyx, the corolla, the androecium and the gynoecium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the flower lacks one whorl, so it is incomplete — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: the androecium and the gynoecium are called the essential whorls of a flower.

answer.model_answer_md: They produce the male and the female gametes needed for sexual reproduction, whereas the calyx and corolla only protect the bud and attract pollinators.

questions.solution_md: Gametes are made by the stamens and carpels.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: the male flower of a pumpkin is called an incomplete flower.

answer.model_answer_md: It lacks one of the four whorls, the gynoecium, although it has the calyx, the corolla and the androecium.

questions.solution_md: Whorl missing.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between actinomorphic and zygomorphic flowers, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **actinomorphic** flower is radially symmetrical: any vertical plane through the centre gives two equal halves, as in **datura**. A **zygomorphic** flower is bilaterally symmetrical: only **one** vertical plane gives equal halves, as in **gulmohar**.

questions.solution_md: Planes of symmetry with examples.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the merous condition of a flower? Name the terms used when the whorls are in threes and in fives, and name the group of plants in which each is typical.

answer.model_answer_md: The **merous condition** is the number of members in each whorl of a flower. Whorls in threes make the flower **trimerous**, typical of **monocots**; whorls in fives make it **pentamerous**, typical of **dicots**.

questions.solution_md: Meaning and two terms.

questions.stem_md: A student records a flower: a small bract at the base of the stalk; five sepals, five petals and five stamens; one gynoecium; equal halves along any vertical plane. Using the terms for describing flowers, describe it in three points.

answer.model_answer_md: The flower is **bracteate**, because it has a bract at the base of the pedicel. It is **pentamerous**, because the sepals, petals and stamens are in fives, and **complete**, because all four whorls, calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, are present. It is **actinomorphic**, since any vertical plane through the centre divides it into equal halves.

questions.solution_md: Bract, merous, completeness, symmetry.

questions.stem_md: Name the four whorls of a flower from outside to inside and state one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **calyx**, made of sepals, protects the bud. The **corolla**, made of petals, is often coloured and attracts pollinators. The **androecium**, made of stamens, produces pollen grains, the male gametophytes. The **gynoecium**, made of carpels, bears the ovules and, after fertilisation, forms the fruit and seeds.

questions.solution_md: Four whorls with functions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a typical flower in longitudinal section, showing the pedicel, thalamus, sepal, petal, stamen and carpel. [3]
(b) Which whorls are essential and which are non-essential? Give one function of each non-essential whorl. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A flower on a **pedicel**; the **thalamus** bearing **sepals** outside, **petals** inside them, **stamens** each with **filament** and **anther**, and in the centre the **carpel** with **stigma**, **style** and **ovary** containing **ovules**; all parts labelled.

(b) The **androecium** and the **gynoecium** are the **essential** whorls, as they produce the gametes. The **calyx** and the **corolla** are the **non-essential** whorls: the calyx **protects** the bud and the corolla **attracts** pollinators.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; essential and non-essential whorls.

questions.solution_md: The standard covers the wings, which in turn cover the keel — option (c).

questions.solution_md: Calyx and corolla that look alike make the perianth, with tepals as members — option (c).

answer.model_answer_md: The large standard petal overlaps the two wings, which overlap the two keel petals, like a flag (vexillum) over the other petals.

questions.solution_md: Standard over wings over keel.

questions.stem_md: Define aestivation. Name any two of its types, giving one plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Aestivation** is the arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud, in relation to the other members of the same whorl. In **valvate** aestivation the margins just touch, as in **Calotropis**; in **twisted** aestivation each member overlaps the next, as in **cotton**.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two types with plants.

questions.stem_md: What is a perianth? Name its members and one plant in which it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: A **perianth** is the calyx and corolla together when they cannot be told apart in colour or form. Its members are called **tepals**, as in the **lily**.

questions.solution_md: Perianth; tepals; lily.

questions.stem_md: What is aestivation? Describe any three of its types, with one plant as an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Aestivation** is the arrangement of petals or sepals in the bud. In **valvate** aestivation the edges of neighbouring members meet without overlapping, as in **Calotropis**. In **twisted** aestivation each member overlaps the next and is overlapped by the previous one, as in **cotton**. In **vexillary** aestivation the large **standard** covers the two **wings**, which cover the **keel**, as in the **pea**.

questions.solution_md: Definition and three types.

questions.stem_md: A gardener says that the petals of datura are joined while those of a rose are free, and that the sepals of both flowers are green. Name the terms for the condition of the corolla in each, and explain what a botanist would call the calyx and corolla of a lily.

answer.model_answer_md: The joined petals of datura make the corolla **gamopetalous**; the free petals of rose make it **polypetalous**. In a lily the sepals and petals are alike in colour and form, so the two whorls together are called a **perianth**, and each member is a **tepal**.

questions.solution_md: Gamopetalous, polypetalous, perianth.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is aestivation? [1]
(b) Draw labelled sketches of the corolla of a pea bud and of a Calotropis bud in transverse section, to show their aestivation. [2]
(c) What is a perianth? Give one example of a plant that has it. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Aestivation** is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud in relation to the other members of the whorl.

(b) **Pea:** the **standard** outside, covering two **wings**, which cover two **keel** petals (**vexillary**). **Calotropis:** five petals whose margins just touch in a ring without overlapping (**valvate**); each sketch is labelled.

(c) A **perianth** is the calyx and the corolla together when they look alike; its members are **tepals**. The **lily** has a perianth.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two sketches; perianth.

questions.stem_md: A student sketches the bud of a five-petalled flower and records, for each petal, how many neighbours it overlaps (O) and how many neighbours overlap it (U): petal 1 (O 2, U 0); petals 2, 3 and 4 (O 1, U 1 each); petal 5 (O 0, U 2). Which conclusion is correct?

options.text_md: The aestivation is twisted, because most petals overlap one neighbour.
The aestivation is valvate, because the totals of O and U are equal.
The aestivation is imbricate: petal 1 is wholly outside and petal 5 wholly inside.
The record is impossible, because the totals of O and U differ.

questions.solution_md: The totals agree (O $= 2+1+1+1+0 = 5$, U $= 0+1+1+1+2 = 5$), so the record is possible. A twisted bud would have O 1 and U 1 for every petal, a valvate bud O 0 and U 0 for every petal; here one petal is wholly outside and one wholly inside, which is imbricate — option (c).

questions.solution_md: One tube of united filaments is monadelphous — option (a).

questions.solution_md: Filaments in more than two bundles are polyadelphous — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Two lobes (thecae) with two sacs each give four sacs — option (b).

questions.solution_md: One floret: $5 \times 4 = 20$; 12 florets: $20 \times 12 = 240$.

questions.stem_md: In a pea flower nine of the ten stamens are joined and one is free. How many filaments are joined into bundles in 8 such flowers?
Distinguish between cohesion and adhesion of stamens, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cohesion** is the union of stamens with **one another**, as in the **monadelphous** stamens of hibiscus. **Adhesion** is the union of stamens with **another whorl** of the flower, as in the **epipetalous** stamens of datura, attached to the petals.

questions.solution_md: Cohesion and adhesion with examples.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a dithecous and a monothecous anther on the number of lobes and of pollen sacs, and name a plant with each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **dithecous** anther has **two lobes** joined by a connective and **four** pollen sacs, as in sunflower. A **monothecous** anther is kidney-shaped, with **one lobe** and **two** pollen sacs, as in hibiscus.

questions.solution_md: Lobes and sacs.

questions.stem_md: Describe three conditions of cohesion in the androecium, giving one plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md: In **monadelphous** stamens all the filaments are joined into **one** bundle, as in **hibiscus**. In **diadelphous** stamens they form **two** bundles, nine joined and one free, as in **pea**. In **syngenesious** stamens only the **anthers** are joined and the filaments are free, as in **sunflower**.

questions.solution_md: Three conditions with plants.

questions.stem_md: A student examines the flower of a datura and of a lily and finds that the stamens of each are attached to another whorl. Name the two conditions and explain how they differ.

answer.model_answer_md: In **datura** the stamens are attached to the petals of the corolla tube, so they are **epipetalous**. In **lily** the stamens are attached to the **tepals** of the perianth, so they are **epiphyllous**. Both are examples of **adhesion**, the union of stamens with another whorl, but they differ in the whorl to which the stamens are attached.

questions.solution_md: Epipetalous, epiphyllous, adhesion.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a dithecous anther in transverse section. [2]
(b) Name three conditions of cohesion of stamens, with one plant for each. [2]
(c) How many pollen sacs are there in a flower with 20 stamens that are monothecous? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Two **lobes (thecae)** joined by the **connective**, each lobe containing two **pollen sacs**, all labelled.

(b) **Monadelphous** (hibiscus), **diadelphous** (pea) and **syngenesious** (sunflower); other conditions are polyadelphous (Bombax) and synandrous (pumpkin).

(c) A monothecous anther has **2** pollen sacs, so the flower has 20 × 2 = **40** pollen sacs.

questions.stem_md: A chamber of the ovary is called a ______.
questions.solution_md: Locule.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The gynoecium of a tomato flower, in which the carpels are fused, is described as syncarpous.
questions.solution_md: True: fused carpels make the gynoecium syncarpous.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The ovary of a sunflower floret is inferior.

**Reason (R):** The thalamus of the sunflower floret fuses with the ovary, so that the other whorls arise above it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: when the thalamus encloses and fuses with the ovary, the other whorls arise above it and the ovary is inferior — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: the ovary of a rose flower is described as half-inferior.

answer.model_answer_md: It lies in a cup-shaped thalamus whose rim bears the other whorls at its level, so it is neither wholly above nor wholly below them.

questions.solution_md: Cup-shaped thalamus.

marking_scheme.step: Ovary in a cup with whorls on the rim

questions.stem_md: A syncarpous ovary with axile placentation has 5 locules and 12 ovules in each locule. How many ovules does the ovary have?
A sunflower head has 600 florets, and each ovary has one ovule at its base. If five of every six ovules develop into seeds, how many seeds does the head produce?
Distinguish between hypogynous and epigynous flowers on the position of the ovary, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **hypogynous** flower the ovary is **superior** and the other whorls arise **below** it, as in **mustard**. In an **epigynous** flower the ovary is **inferior**, because the thalamus fuses with it, and the other whorls arise **above** it, as in **sunflower**.

questions.solution_md: Ovary position with examples.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an apocarpous and a syncarpous gynoecium, giving one plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md: In an **apocarpous** gynoecium the carpels are **free** from one another, each with its own ovary, as in **lotus**. In a **syncarpous** gynoecium the carpels are **fused** into one compound ovary with chambers called **locules**, as in **tomato**.

questions.solution_md: Free and fused carpels.

questions.stem_md: A botanist examines three flowers in longitudinal section. In flower P the sepals, petals and stamens arise below the ovary; in Q they arise from the rim of a cup round the ovary; in R they arise above the ovary. Name the condition of each flower, state the position of its ovary and give one example.

answer.model_answer_md: **P** is **hypogynous**: the ovary is **superior**, as in mustard. **Q** is **perigynous**: the ovary is **half-inferior**, in a cup-shaped thalamus, as in rose. **R** is **epigynous**: the thalamus is fused with the ovary, which is **inferior**, as in sunflower or cucumber.

questions.solution_md: Three flowers.

questions.stem_md: Define placentation. Describe the axile, parietal and basal types, with one plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Placentation** is the arrangement of **ovules** on the **placenta** inside the ovary. In **axile** placentation the ovules are on a central axis of a chambered ovary, as in **tomato**. In **parietal** placentation they lie on the inner wall of a one-chambered ovary, as in **mustard**. In **basal** placentation a single ovule is attached at the base, as in **sunflower**.

questions.solution_md: Definition and three types.

questions.stem_md: A student compares a pea ovary with a Dianthus ovary and finds the ovules of the first along one margin of a single chamber, and those of the second on a central column without partitions. Name the placentation of each and explain how the two differ.

answer.model_answer_md: The pea shows **marginal** placentation: the ovules are borne along one **margin** of a one-chambered, single-carpelled ovary. *Dianthus* shows **free central** placentation: the ovules are borne on a **central column** that is not joined to the wall by partitions. They differ in the position of the ovules: on the margin of the ovary, or on a column in its centre.

questions.solution_md: Marginal; free central; difference.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a flower in longitudinal section to show hypogynous condition. [2]
(b) Distinguish between an apocarpous and a syncarpous gynoecium. [1]
(c) Name the placentation of tomato and of sunflower and state where the ovules are borne in each. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A thalamus with the **sepals, petals and stamens** attached **below** a **superior ovary**, which bears the **style** and **stigma**; the parts are labelled.

(b) An **apocarpous** gynoecium has **free** carpels; a **syncarpous** gynoecium has **fused** carpels, usually with chambers.

(c) **Tomato** shows **axile** placentation, the ovules on the central axis of a chambered ovary. **Sunflower** shows **basal** placentation, one ovule at the base of a one-chambered ovary.

questions.solution_md: Hypogynous flower; carpels; placentation.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is placentation? Name the five types. [2]
(b) Draw labelled diagrams of an ovary in transverse section to show axile and parietal placentation. [2]
(c) Which type of placentation is shown by pea? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Placentation** is the arrangement of **ovules** on the **placenta** in the ovary. The types are **axile, parietal, free central, basal** and **marginal**.

(b) **Axile:** a round ovary divided into chambers by partitions meeting at the centre, with ovules on the **central axis**. **Parietal:** a one-chambered ovary with ovules on the **inner wall**; the placenta and ovules are labelled.

(c) The pea ovary shows **marginal** placentation, with ovules along one margin of the single chamber.

questions.solution_md: Definition and types; two diagrams; pea.

questions.stem_md: In a radish shoot the main axis keeps growing and bears flowers on its sides; the flowers at the base opened first and the buds are near the tip. The inflorescence is
questions.solution_md: An axis that keeps growing, with the oldest flowers at the base, is racemose — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On a jasmine branch the main axis ends in a flower, which opened first, and the younger flowers lie below it on side branches. The inflorescence is
questions.solution_md: An axis that ends in a flower, with the oldest flower at the top, is cymose — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The terminal flower of a cymose inflorescence is the last one to open.
questions.solution_md: False: in a cymose inflorescence the terminal flower is the oldest and opens first.

questions.stem_md: The opening of flowers from the base towards the tip of the axis, as in a raceme, is called ______ succession.
questions.solution_md: Acropetal.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: the main axis of a cymose inflorescence does not keep growing in length.

answer.model_answer_md: Its main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited.

questions.solution_md: Axis ends in a flower.

questions.stem_md: Define inflorescence. State two differences between racemose and cymose inflorescence.

answer.model_answer_md: An **inflorescence** is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis. In a **racemose** inflorescence the main axis **keeps growing** and the **oldest flowers are at the base**; in a **cymose** one the axis **ends in a flower** and the **oldest flower is at the top**.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two differences.

questions.stem_md: A florist has a bunch of radish shoots and a bunch of jasmine shoots. Explain how she can tell the two inflorescences apart by looking at the main axis and at the order in which the flowers open.

answer.model_answer_md: In **radish** the main axis **keeps growing** and bears flowers on its sides, so the inflorescence is **racemose**; the **oldest flowers are at the base** and the youngest near the tip. In **jasmine** the main axis **ends in a flower**, so the inflorescence is **cymose**; the **oldest flower is at the top** and the younger flowers lie below it.

questions.solution_md: Main axis and order of opening.

marking_scheme.step: Jasmine: axis ends in a flower, cymose

questions.stem_md: A raceme has 30 flowers and one flower opens every 3 days, starting from the base. How many flowers are open on day 30, counting the one that opened on day 0?
questions.solution_md: $30 \div 3 + 1 = 11$ flowers open, so 19 buds are still closed.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define inflorescence. [1]
(b) Draw labelled diagrams of a racemose and of a cymose inflorescence, numbering the flowers in the order of opening. [2]
(c) In a raceme of 18 flowers, one flower opens every 2 days from the base upward. How many days pass between the opening of the lowest and the topmost flower? [1]
(d) Name one plant with a racemose inflorescence. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An **inflorescence** is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.

(b) **Racemose:** a main axis that keeps growing, with flowers numbered **1 at the base** and the highest numbers near the tip. **Cymose:** a main axis that ends in a flower numbered **1**, with younger flowers numbered below it.

(c) There are 17 gaps between 18 flowers, so 17 × 2 = **34 days**.

(d) **Radish** (or the golden shower tree).
